title: Your Kid Can Get Every Answer Right and Still Not Know How to Think
author: Shari Keller
summary: Shari Keller distinguishes between two skills that are frequently conflated in both classroom and home learning: producing a correct fact and evaluating what that fact actually means. Anchored by her own childhood memory of her father walking her through base-2, base-8, and base-16 counting systems rather than dismissing her question about why numbers use ten digits, and by a later example of one of her own children iteratively redesigning a college soil-aeration experiment after an unexpected result, Keller argues that most instructional interactions default to recall (fixed answers waiting to be retrieved) rather than reasoning (weighing evidence, explaining mechanism, defending interpretation), and that this default is a habit, not a necessity. Her practical intervention is a set of paired question swaps across history, math, and literature that convert a fact-retrieval question into an evaluation question with the same content, framed as requiring only three to ten extra seconds of adult attention rather than a curriculum overhaul. She closes with a distinction between 'interrogation,' a question asked to check whether a child arrives at an answer the adult already holds, and genuine 'inquiry,' a question asked because the adult truly does not know what the child will say, arguing children can immediately sense which one they are being asked.
points: Keller's central distinction, producing a fact versus evaluating one, reframes a common parenting and teaching assumption: that a correct answer indicates learning, when it may only indicate successful retrieval without any accompanying reasoning skill.

Her own father's response to a first-grade place-value question (teaching base-2, base-8, and base-16 systems on the spot rather than saying 'that's just how numbers work') is used as the essay's founding example of turning a fact into a genuinely questioned convention.

The soil-experiment anecdote demonstrates the transferable, later-life payoff of this habit: her son's ability to treat an unexpected experimental result as something to investigate (missing variables) rather than something to accept or discard is framed as a direct descendant of earlier fact-versus-reasoning practice.

Her subject-specific question swaps (history: 'whose version would you trust less, and why?'; math: 'why does the method work at all?'; literature: 'what does that choice tell you about who they are?') give a portable, immediately usable technique rather than an abstract principle.

Her interrogation-versus-inquiry distinction adds a crucial caveat often missing from 'ask better questions' advice: a question only builds reasoning skill if the adult genuinely does not know the answer they expect, since children can detect and discount rhetorical questions aimed at confirming a predetermined answer.
quotes: Not what's the answer, why is that the answer. You've got about three seconds to decide whether to hand over the quick version or actually get into it.
My dad didn't tell me "that's just how numbers work." He asked me if I wanted to know why. Then he walked me through counting in base 2, base 8, base 16.
Your kid doesn't need to know more facts. They need practice deciding what the facts actually mean.

He didn't get there just by running more trials. He got there by rethinking what those trials actually measured, then treating every unexpected result as something to investigate instead of something to accept or throw out.

The first one asks them to retrieve something that's already fixed: a name, a formula, a plot point. The second asks them to construct something that isn't just sitting there waiting: weigh evidence, explain a method, defend an interpretation. That's the real difference between recall and reasoning.

A question asked to check whether your kid landed on the answer you already have in mind is interrogation, even if it's phrased as "what do you think?" A question asked because you genuinely don't know what they'll say, and you're willing to hear wherever they land, is inquiry.
You'll be helping them become a kid who can think instead of a kid who can just answer.
